source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Alfalfa — emissions_per_kg: LCA literature places irrigated US alfalfa at 0.2–0.4 kg CO2e/kg. P&N 2018 meta-analysis of 38,700 farms covers all major animal feed crops; alfalfa's low-emission profile is driven by nitrogen-fixation (reducing synthetic N fertilizer demand), perennial root system (low tillage), and high yield diluting per-kg fixed costs. Value of 0.4 kg CO2e/kg represents the upper bound for commercially irrigated alfalfa (irrigation energy is the dominant emission source in water-intensive production regions such as California's Central Valley). CORRECTION 2026-09-24: P&N 2018 does not report alfalfa (no forage products in Supplementary Table S1), so 0.4 is not a P&N number; it comes from unspecified LCA literature. It is already a crop-production (farm-gate) figure, not cradle-to-retail. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: FAO — Alfalfa Crop Information
source.note: Alfalfa — emissions_per_kg: FAO crop information confirms alfalfa's low GHG footprint relative to other forage crops due to biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) reducing synthetic N2O emissions and perennial growth habit reducing tillage-related CO2. Consistent with LCA studies reporting 0.2–0.35 kg CO2e/kg for rain-fed or minimally irrigated systems; 0.35 used as a conservative midpoint for globally mixed production. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the cited FAO crop-information URL now returns 404, and FAO's crop-information pages cover water and yield, not GHG; the 0.35 could not be verified. It is a crop-production (farm-gate) figure. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Alfalfa — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg: same 0.4 as emissions_per_kg, because that value is ALREADY farm gate (crop production only: fertiliser, irrigation energy, machinery; no processing/packaging/retail). Land-use change not included (perennial forage on established land; small). Not a P&N value — see correction on emissions_per_kg. Confidence 2. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

Converted to as-fed hay at ~10% moisture: 0.17 x 0.90 = 0.15. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Grass hay — emissions_per_kg: LCA literature places perennial grass hay at 0.15–0.35 kg CO2e/kg. P&N 2018 covers all major livestock feed crops; grass hay's low emission profile reflects its perennial growth (low annual tillage), minimal nitrogen fertilizer need relative to annual crops, and moderate yield. Emissions are dominated by fertilizer N2O (for improved pastures) and machinery fuel. Value of 0.3 kg CO2e/kg is consistent with LCA estimates for mixed US grass hay production. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: P&N 2018 does not report grass hay (no forage products in Supplementary Table S1), so 0.3 is not a P&N number; it comes from unspecified LCA literature. It is already a crop-production (farm-gate) figure. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: FAO GLEAM — Global Livestock Environmental Assessment Model
source.note: Grass hay — emissions_per_kg: FAO GLEAM v3.0 provides feed-crop GHG intensities as part of livestock supply chain LCAs. Grass hay and pasture forages are consistently among the lowest-emission feed inputs due to perennial root systems, low synthetic fertilizer inputs, and high carbon sequestration in permanent grassland soils. GLEAM feed-crop estimates for perennial grasses range 0.15–0.3 kg CO2e/kg; 0.25 represents the global production-weighted average for improved permanent grassland hay.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Grass hay — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg: same 0.3 as emissions_per_kg, because that value is ALREADY farm gate (fertiliser N2O + machinery fuel; no processing/packaging/retail). LUC not included (permanent grassland). Not a P&N value — see correction on emissions_per_kg. Confidence 2. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

source.note: Grass hay — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg (US): Adom et al. 2012 US national average 160 g CO2e/kg DRY 'forage mix' (the closest category to grass hay; cradle to farm gate; no land-use change). Converted to as-fed at ~12% moisture: 0.16 x 0.88 = 0.14. Confidence 2 because 'forage mix' is not pure grass hay. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

source.note: Fishmeal — nutrition: Feed-grade fishmeal (low-temperature/steam-dried) proximate composition per gram: protein 0.60–0.70, fat 0.08–0.12, ash 0.15–0.20, moisture ~0.10. Human nutritional database values are not applicable (feed ingredient); macros derived from standard fishmeal product specifications reported in the FAO aquaculture sector documentation.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fishmeal — yield_fraction: Set to 1.0 because fishmeal is used as-is in feed formulations with no further edible-fraction processing step; the entire product is the functional feed ingredient.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fishmeal — emissions_per_kg: FAO fleet-level emission intensities for small pelagic capture fisheries (anchovy, sardine, herring) average 0.9–1.2 kg CO2e/kg landed fish for purse-seine operations. At a FIFO conversion of ~4.5 kg wet fish per kg fishmeal, vessel fuel emissions alone reach 4.0–5.4 kg CO2e/kg fishmeal. Adding fishmeal plant drying and processing energy (~0.5–1.0 kg CO2e/kg) gives a total range of 5–7 kg CO2e/kg. Central estimate 6.0 kg CO2e/kg used as a production-weighted midpoint across major fishmeal-producing nations (Peru, Chile, Denmark, Norway). CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the derivation is ~10-20x too high. Its premise that small-pelagic purse-seine fisheries emit 0.9–1.2 kg CO2e/kg landed conflicts with fishery LCAs: Peruvian anchoveta (the largest fishmeal fishery) emits 0.088–0.109 kg CO2e/kg landed and Peruvian fishmeal ~0.32 kg CO2e/kg meal cradle-to-export (Deville et al. 2025, source 277). The 4.5:1 fish-to-meal ratio is fine; the fuel intensity is not. Confidence lowered 3 -> 1.

source.title: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) — Feeding Farmed Salmon: Is Organic Better? (Aquaculture)
source.note: Fishmeal — emissions_per_kg: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) LCA of Norwegian Atlantic salmon feeds reports cradle-to-feed-mill emissions for conventional fishmeal at 5.0–8.0 kg CO2e/kg, central estimate ~6.5 kg CO2e/kg. Variability driven by source fishery fuel efficiency, drying technology (steam vs. direct-fire), and geographic origin. Consistent with the FAO fleet-level estimate (source 74) of 6.0 kg CO2e/kg. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: could not be verified: the URL's ScienceDirect pii (S0044848607009829) does not match Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) 'Feeding farmed salmon: Is organic better?' (Aquaculture 272:399–416, pii S0044848607005169), and a 5–8 kg CO2e/kg fishmeal range is an order of magnitude above recent fishmeal LCAs (~0.3 kg CO2e/kg, source 277). Confidence lowered 3 -> 1.

source.title: Deville et al. (2025) — Identifying current trends in the environmental impacts linked to fishmeal and fish oil production in Peru (Aquaculture 600:742239)
source.note: Fishmeal — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg: Deville et al. 2025 LCA of a Peruvian producer (~10% of national output; 169 anchoveta vessels, 4 plants, 2019 and 2021): ~320 kg CO2e per t fishmeal, energy allocation between meal and oil. Stages included: fishing (fuel ~45% of the total), reduction (cooking, pressing, drying — the processing step, included because animals eat the processed meal) and export transport. No land-use change applies. Existing emissions_per_kg is already cradle-to-feed-mill (no retail stages), but its magnitude is wrong — see correction. Confidence 2: single country (Peru is the largest producer and among the lowest-carbon); North-Atlantic fishmeal and plants on heavy fuel oil are higher, so the global mean is probably somewhat above 0.32. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fish oil — nutrition: Feed-grade fish oil is 100% lipid with no protein, fiber, or carbohydrate. Caloric density ~9.0 kcal/g (lipid energy standard). Saturated fat fraction approximately 27% of total fat for pelagic fish oil blends (anchovy/sardine/herring); EPA+DHA make up 25–35% of total fatty acids. Human nutritional database values are not applicable (feed ingredient); macros derived from standard fish oil product specifications in FAO aquaculture sector documentation.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fish oil — yield_fraction: Set to 1.0 because fish oil is used as-is in feed formulations; the entire product is the functional feed ingredient.

source.title: FAO (2014) — Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sectors
source.note: Fish oil — emissions_per_kg: Fish oil is a co-product of fishmeal production at a yield ratio of roughly 1 kg oil per 5 kg fishmeal (by weight). Under economic allocation (oil valued at 2–3× fishmeal per kg due to omega-3 EFA content), fish oil receives approximately 35–55% of total upstream capture and processing emissions. Applying this allocation to the 5–7 kg CO2e/kg fishmeal footprint and scaling to oil yield gives ~2.5–4.0 kg CO2e/kg oil. Central estimate 3.5 kg CO2e/kg used, consistent with published aquaculture feed LCA studies using economic co-product allocation. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the derivation scales an overstated fishmeal footprint (5–7 kg CO2e/kg; see fishmeal correction) and its source-74 text mixes mass and economic allocation shares. The 3.5 result happens to be near a direct LCA value (Peru, 4.43 kg CO2e/kg oil under energy allocation; source 277) but is not independently supported. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) — Feeding Farmed Salmon: Is Organic Better? (Aquaculture)
source.note: Fish oil — emissions_per_kg: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) report fish oil at 3.0–5.0 kg CO2e/kg under economic allocation (central estimate ~4.0 kg CO2e/kg) from the same cradle-to-feed-mill boundary used for fishmeal. Economic allocation is applied because fish oil commands a significant price premium over fishmeal per kg, driven by its omega-3 EFA (EPA/DHA) content which is the primary limiting nutrient in high-performance salmonid feeds. Corroborates the 3.5 kg CO2e/kg central estimate from source 74. CORRECTION 2026-09-24: the URL's ScienceDirect pii (S0044848607009829) does not match Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) (pii S0044848607005169), so the 3.0–5.0 range could not be checked. Confidence lowered 3 -> 2.

source.title: Deville et al. (2025) — Identifying current trends in the environmental impacts linked to fishmeal and fish oil production in Peru (Aquaculture 600:742239)
source.note: Fish oil — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg: Deville et al. 2025 Peruvian LCA: ~4,430 kg CO2e per t crude fish oil, energy allocation between fishmeal and oil. Stages included: fishing, reduction/oil separation, export transport. No land-use change. Confidence 2: single country, and the allocation choice drives the meal/oil split. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.

source.title: Pelletier & Tyedmers (2007) — Feeding Farmed Salmon: Is Organic Better? (Aquaculture)
source.note: Fish oil — farm_gate_emissions_per_kg: same 4.0 as emissions_per_kg, which is ALREADY a cradle-to-feed-mill figure (fishing + reduction; no retail stages). Unverified source — see correction on emissions_per_kg. Confidence 2. Added 2026-09-24 so animal feed is charged farm-gate, not retail, emissions.
